The Piedmont Fire Department responded to a “high stakes” house fire at 660 Blair Avenue on Tuesday night, April 9 at 11:10 p.m. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan stated that when his crew arrived, the fire was “hazardous” and “devastating” due to the severity of the damage sustained and the fact that the fire had begun to spread to a neighboring home. Because the homeowner was unable to be located at the time, firefighters had to assume that she was still inside and took heightened risks to ensure her safety. Luckily, a thorough search of the house revealed that no one was inside. The owner was later discovered to be on vacation out of the country. Officials are still investigating the cause of Piedmont’s second major house fire in as many months. station at 11:11 a.m., Fire Captain Justin McNulty knew the house fire would be a problem. “As soon as we turned out of the station, we could already see a glow on the hill coming from the house on fire and a column of black smoke above it,” McNulty said. When firefighters arrived, Piedmont police had already closed off the area. The entire bottom story and left side of the house was on fire, and a second-story window was sending fire toward a neighboring house that was smoking and smoldering. Fire Lieutenant Zach Heliker took over as Incident Commander, and two teams were formed – one to fight the initial fire and another to prevent it from spreading to neighboring homes. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, April 18 at the Piedmont Community Church Guild Hall. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now- such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impacts also continue for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver award – the highest honor for volunteers – will be presented to Lisa Gros, a mainstay of Troop 6 and former President of the Piedmont Council. The selection committee was chaired by Chris Lee and included many longstanding Piedmont leaders. Gros was chosen for her depth and breadth of service- she served as council president during her board tenure; has served as a dedicated assistant scoutmaster that includes leading a trek through the boundary waters of Minnesota and Canada; and has served as a Webelos den leader to help younger scouts make the transition to a troop. She has provided outstanding support to the Order of the Arrow (honor society for Scouts BSA), and also volunteered with the High Adventure Crew. She has consistently demonstrated cheerful service through irksome tasks and weighty responsibilities. “Working with youth, not only your own child, is one of the most meaningful legacies you can leave,” said Gros. “It’s also a great way to meet other really cool adults.” The council will also recognize many other volunteers who have served in some cases for many, many years. The dinner is open to community members and tickets are available online at www.piedmontbsa.org. For more information contact Kate Benson, Executive Director, at 547-4493. articles.text: “The Lord is my shepherd: I shall not want. He has me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside still waters.” In his delightful book The Psalms: A Guide for the Heart and Soul, my friend Rabbi Allan Berkowitz begins his reflection on the 23rd Psalm with these words. “Is there a Psalm with greater brand recognition than Psalm 23? Its opening verse, The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want, is universally familiar. Psalm 23 evokes pathos, thus it is recited at funerals and is borne deeply in many hearts as a comforting mantra for God’s personal protection. It is a poetic blanket that wraps us in warmth and comfort. One of the enduring images of this warm and comforting poetic blanket is that of being led to rest in green pastures. This portrait is consistent with the poet’s experience. It is also a vision that is familiar to residents of the East Bay in the spring as we look toward the verdant hills dotted with orange poppies. It is an image of serenity, abundance, protection and provision. On Earth Sunday 2024, I invite us all to contemplate green pastures. To call to mind a mental image of the psalmist’s words. Green pastures represent the earth as it is, beautiful yet oh so vulnerable. They represent the earth as it can be, a safe home for all living things, a garden in which all things bright and beautiful grow, a paradise in which all creatures great and small thrive. They all represent the peril before us. The green pastures of our planet are not doing very well. It is important to note that green pastures are an ecological imperative. In addition to beauty, they provide oxygen, food for many species, protection to organisms seen and unseen, stability to the soil, connections for watersheds and cover for the aquifers below. It is important to note that green pastures are vulnerable. They are disappearing at alarming rates. Many species are endangered because of the loss of habitat. If green pastures disappear, can thriving human communities be far behind?

articles.text: In its 45th year, the annual Betty C. Howard Award was presented by the Recreation Department to Carolyn Yang Stewart and Madison Mills. The Award is given to staff and community members who exemplify outstanding volunteer achievement. In addition to her duties at the Recreation Department, Stewart serves as the ultimate frisbee coach for the Piedmont Middle School team. Madison, a former Piedmont High varsity player, serves as the basketball coach for Piedmont Middle School. The ceremony took place in City Hall on April 1. Many members of the PMS ultimate frisbee team, Purple Reign, were there to show support. The two awardees were introduced by Sports Coordinator Akil Danjuma. “The Betty C. Howard Award symbolizes more than just recognition of service. It is a celebration of individuals who have profoundly impacted their communities through their dedication and spirit,” said Danjuma. The Betty C. Howard Award was established in 1979 by Recreation Director Mark Delventhal to honor a longtime key member of the staff. Originally a parttime worker, Howard eventually worked in the department for nearly 30 years, cultivating a reputation for kindness and commitment to the department. “Betty Howard was iconic within the Recreation Department,“ said Delventhal, who created the award. “She was sort of like a mother figure to a lot of people in the department, including the directors.” He explained that the award was meant to honor Howard’s dual legacy of dedication to the department and volunteering in the community. “Once a year we gave an award for an outstanding staff member, almost always a partPhotos by Jesse Rosenberg Carolyn Yang Stewart wins Betty C. Howard Award. time staff member who was the backbone of the department in a lot of ways, and then a volunteer in the community, particularly in the sports area,” he said. Danjuma described the basis for selecting Stewart and Mills for the Award. “Since 2016, Carolyn Yang-Stewart has led the Piedmont Middle School ultimate Frisbee team, Purple Rain, with unparalleled dedication and skill, Coach Mills exemplifies what it means to be a beacon of commitment, passion, and energy in the community of Piedmont. Her passion for basketball as a tool to give back to her community embodies the very essence of this award,” he said. Stewart assumed head coaching responsibilities of the PMS team in 2016 following the departure of Kevin Lee, a friend and Piedmont resident. articles.text: Photos by City of Piedmont Contractors with the company OneSource clear vegetation above the Corporation yard. Last week, contractors began clearing vegetation on the hills above the Corporation Yard for fire safety reasons, according to the Public Works Department. Laborers are currently working their way up the hill to remove vegetation that could pose a fire risk in the hotter summer months. This work has been requested by members of the Maxwelton neighborhood in recent years and is part of a larger initiative by the Public Works Department and Piedmont Fire Department to reduce fire risk in “the highest priority locations” across the city. “Our goal is to prevent fire from being able to spread from point A to point B around the City,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “In this case, we don’t want the uphill travel of fire from a lower area in this topography up to the higher levels where there are residents and houses.” Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works, agreed with Brannigan about the project’s importance. “The topography makes it particularly onerous because it is so steep. Fire could spread very quickly, and we have a neighborhood above it,” said Gonzales. He also mentioned that the 1991 East Bay Hills Fire ended only a few hundred yards from the area, which was a close call for the entire city of Piedmont. According to Gonzales, the work is especially dangerous for the contractors due to the steep slopes and the difficulty of using equipment such as chainsaws, industrial vehicles, and other power tools. To keep workers from losing balance and injuring themselves, contractors are frequently required to anchor to a stable piece of the landscape using a harness or other methods. The city awarded the contract for the vegetation management project to a private company, OneSource, in January but only started clearing the dense vegetation last week due to the risk of soil erosion posed by the recent rains. “We don’t want to start removing vegetation when there’s a high probability of rain and erosion that can occur. So, we’ve been looking to time it for after the rain but before the fire season, if that makes sense,” said Gonzales. The goats, however, will still return. Officials hope that this effort will make the annual vegetation clearing done by goats in the summer more effective, as well as provide a critical buffer for homes on the hill in the event of a fire. Heavy machinery is being used to clear away vegetation that poses a fire risk to the Maxwelton neighborhood.

articles.text: Earlier this month, the last total solar eclipse visible from the United States until 2044 took place. Observers near or within the path of the eclipse celebrated the celestial event, each experiencing the phenomenon from their own unique perspective. Depending on where they were, people had the chance to see either a total solar eclipse or a partial solar eclipse, and both were a stellar sight to see. What’s the difference? A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, fully blocking the face of the Sun. During a partial solar eclipse, only part of the Sun is blocked by the Moon. Did you know the Sun is about 400 times bigger than the Moon? It’s also about 400 times farther from Earth than the Moon. That is why, when we observe a total solar eclipse, the Moon appears to be the same size as the Sun from our view on Earth. What is the path of totality? During a total solar eclipse, the Moon’s shadow is projected onto the Earth’s surface. Every time there is an eclipse, the shadow lands in a different place. This is also known as the path of totality. The path of totality is where the Sun appears completely blocked by the Moon. The path of totality for the solar eclipse that took place earlier this month on April 8, 2024, had a 115-mile-wide path. The path extended across Mexico and the middle and northern part of the United States, where it crossed 15 states from Texas to Maine. Observing from the Bay Area This explains why Bay Area observers witnessed a partial solar eclipse instead of a total solar eclipse. California was outside the path of totality, and although we did not observe a total solar eclipse, we did have the chance to witness about 45% totality in the Bay Area. There are plenty more astronomical events in store this year for Bay Area observers. Stay tuned for more upcoming viewing events at Chabot Space & Science Center. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a nonprofit institution, community resource and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.

articles.text: PFD to defend their title against other First Responder units The Piedmont Fire Department (PFD) will compete against other Bay Area fire departments in this year’s Big Climb on Saturday, May 4, as part of the First Responder Challenge, a fundraiser for the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society. The event is a competitive race up a series of stairs at Oracle Park. Participants will compete for time on a course that spans the stadium’s upper deck, descends its ramps, and finishes near the stadium’s entrance on Second Street. Last year, Piedmont won the first responder division in both the team and individual categories. They will have to defend their title this year as they go against the fire departments from San Francisco, San Mateo, and others. “We’ve done a lot of different fitness things over the years, whether it was CrossFit competitions or the Firefighter Challenge, which is an agility course,” explained Fire Captain Justin McNulty. “This competition came up last year for the first time when a local resident suggested it to us,” McNulty added. McNulty was the obvious choice to be part of a team from Piedmont. A self-described “fitness nut,” he regularly competes in physical competitions on his own time, including several running and CrossFit challenges each year. McNulty has also gained a reputation within his department for fitness running the annual 5K Piedmont Turkey Trot in full turnout gear at least half a dozen times. “I even had them change out my air bottle at the top of the hill on Sea View before I finished the course,” he told the Post. Last year marked the first time the Big Climb included a First Responders division, and the new category has already sparked friendly competition among local fire departments. “I might be a little biased being with San Francisco Fire, but currently we’re the best at the stair climbs,” said San Francisco Fire Captain Jonathan Baxter. “I remember hearing that last year and thinking, ‘You don’t know what you’re doing, guys. You’re poking the bear,’” joked McNulty. The Piedmont Fire Department’s team this year includes Justin McNulty, Brittany Borges, Nikolas Christ, Brandon Clupny, Christopher Kruger, Brian Protheroe, Anthony Renteria, and Nadder Shehadeh. Erica Melgarejo, an event organizer with the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society explained that the First Responder Challenge is a great way for her organization to increase participation in its events, as well as inspire competition among departments for a good cause. “In the future, we hope to have even more departments join us at Big Climb in SF alongside other competitors to help take down blood cancer,” she explained. At the time of writing, the Piedmont Fire Department ranks fourth in fundraising under the “corporate donor” catagory with $1,159.47. To learn more about the Big Climb in San Francisco or to donate to the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, visit lls.org/ big-climb. Staff Photo Capt. Justin McNulty (left), Brittany Borges, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, and Anthony Renteria hold last year’s trophies from the Big Climb 2023. But PHS came alive in the top of the fourth, scoring three runs to take the lead and tacked on another four in the top fifth. Arroyo added individual runs in the fifth, sixth, and bottom seventh. In the top of the first, Peter Krumins knocked in Will Parker on a ground ball through the infield to centerfield for the opening run with two outs. But Arroyo assumed a 3-1 lead by the top of the fourth. That’s when PHS when ahead with a three run inning, starting with Shafer Dando getting hit by a pitch and Brandon Dicke drawing a walk. With one out, Jack Meyjes singled in Dando, while Markos Lagios slugged a two-run double to left field, 4-3. In the following top of the fifth, PHS loaded the bases with Krumins reaching on an error, while Dando and Dicke smacked singles. Diego Delventhal then grounded into a fielder’s choice, scoring Vo to make it a comfortable 8-3 lead. The Dons tacked on runs in the bottom of the fifth, sixth, and seventh to bring the score closer 8-6. In the bottom of the seventh, Arroyo had the bases loaded with just one out, Dimitri Papahadjopolous forced a double-play, where Krumins fielded at shortstop, turned to Delventhal at second base, gunning out the batter at first to end the ballgame. The Dons entered the seventh inning trailing 6-5 but scored the game-winner in walk-off fashion. It marked a strong performance by first-year varsity player Samantha Ronen with two RBIs and a double. articles.text: From January 2021 We return to one of our hikes in 2021 where you can find groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees in Portola State Park. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than most others found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within Portola Redwoods. Aside from the awe striking size, the thousand year old tree is among the few old growths to make it Hikers can still spot the char marks from fires from previous decades among the redwoods in Portola Redwoods State Park. Downed trees line your path on many of the 18 miles of hiking trails at Portola Redwoods State Park.

articles.text: In celebration of South African Freedom Day, SF JAZZ welcomes South African saxophonist McCoy Mrubata to the Miner Auditorium stage for two performances on Sunday, April 28. Mrubata hails from Cape Town’s historic Langa township and grew up with the sounds of African music, including the soulful hymns of the Zion Church, the chants and rhythms of traditional healers and the music of the Merry Macs band. In the aftermath of the 1976 uprising in South Africa, Mrubata studied informally under Langa greats like Madoda Gxabeka, Winston Ngozi, the Ngcukanas, Ezra and Duke, Blackie Tempi and Robert Sithole. By the early 1980s he was playing in cover bands like Fever, Touch, Airborne and Vukani. He gained international fame in 1992 when he toured the world with Hugh Masekela’s Lerapo band. He has collaborated with Brazilian artists Airto and Flora Purim. McCoy’s albums have won numerous awards, including McCoy Mrubata the South African Music Award for best traditional jazz release. Concerts are held at 6 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. Visit https:// www.sfjazz.org/tickets/productions/23-24/mccoy-mrubata/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Tickets are still available for San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SF MOMA) Art Bash, the museum’s biggest annual fundraiser. The event helps fund SFMOMA’s education, family programs and community engagement events, benefiting over 150,000 people every year. The fundraiser begins at 5 p.m. with cocktail reception and immersive dinner experience designed by iconic filmmaker and installation artist Isaac Julien. Julien’s filmmaking career began with his celebrated 1989 drama-documentary Looking for Langston, an exploration of the poet Langston Hughes and the Harlem Renaissance. He was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2017 Birthday Honors for services to the arts and was knighted in the 2022 Birthday Honors for services to diversity and inclusion in art. Art Bash 2024 will feature photography and large-scale images from the artist’s series Ten Thousand Waves. The dinner program will be followed by a lounge experience for dinner guests opening at 8 p.m., including Solo to Symphony, a multidisciplinary installation conceived by Bay Area– based artist Richard Misrach, an American photographer known for his portrayal of deserts of the American West. A late-night party begins at 10 p.m. and includes immersive art encounters, live musical performances, museum exhibitions and complimentary food and drink with ticket purchases. The event takes place at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit sfmoma.org/artbash.

articles.text: Selected pieces from SFMOMA’s newest exhibition, Art of Noise, will be on view May 4 through August 18. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) will exhibit Art of Noise, on view May 4 through August 18, to showcase groundbreaking art design that visualizes musical experiences through the decades. Art of Noise will feature over 800 artworks drawn largely from the SFMOMA collection, including 550 posters, 150 album covers, 100 design objects and four large-scale installations that marry design and audio. The exhibition covers more than a century of visual aesthetics from the world of music. “Design has the ability to revolutionize and strengthen our relationship to sound. This unique exhibition shows how trailblazing graphics and design objects fuel our bonds to music and help us develop lasting memories of fleeting musical phenomena,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “Art of Noise also manifests our goal to create captivating exhibitions that connect contemporary culture with art and design from a wide range of makers and perspectives.” Also in the exhibition are music posters by famed artists like Milton Glaser, Victor Moscoso, Bonnie MacLean and Takenobu Igarashi, as well as mid-century modernist record sleeves and album covers by Laini (Sylvia) Abernathy, Emmet McBain, Reid Miles and more. “This exhibition is a chance for visitors to reflect on our collective experience of music as visualized through expressive and often cutting-edge design,” said SFMOMA Associate Curator Joseph Becker. “The San Francisco Bay Area has been an influential center for graphic and industrial design, including audio products that merge aesthetics and engineering, and era-defining posters and fliers. SFMOMA’s design collection reflects these local strengths, as well as iconic designs from around the world, which can be seen in the hundreds of surprising and familiar works on view in Art of Noise.” SFMOMA will host a free “Community Day” on Saturday, May 4, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. where everyone enjoys free admission to the entire museum, and a free “Family Day” on Sunday, June 9 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Up to four adults get in free when accompanied by a child 18 or younger. pages.text: Wednesday, April 17, 2024 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Everybody Knows a stunning film from Spain By Chris Honoré Everybody Knows was written and directed by two-time Iranian Oscar winner Asghar Farhad (Separation and The Salesman). The setting is Spain, in a small village near Madrid. Laura (Penelope Cruz), the oldest daughter in a large extended family, has arrived with her two children from Argentina for the wedding of Laura’s sister, Ana (Inma Cuesta). Her husband, Alejandro (Richard Darin), has not come along, remaining behind, she explains, for business reasons. Initially, the audience is left to try and sort out the many members of this large affectionate and voluble family – Laura’s father and mother, her cousins, nephews, the bride and groom, uncles and aunts. With Laura on the visit is her 16-year-old daughter, Irene (Carla Campra). A bit wild, brimming with life and energy, she instantly begins to flirt with a teenage cousin, Felipe (Sergio Castell Anos), As the arriving family members and guests settle in, Laura’s long ago adolescent crush, Paco (Javier Bardem), a local vintner, arrives to warmly welcome Laura and kids home. All is deliciously wonderful and quickly transitions to the wedding filled with Catholic liturgy, ringing bells, followed by a celebratory party. During a long night of dancing, drinking, and eating, Irene is taken sick, and with Laura in tow goes to her room to rest. She A scene from Asghar Mailet-Guy’s Everybody Knows is left alone to nap and Laura returns to the party. Later, going upstairs to check on Irene, she discovers that her daughter is not in her room. Finding Paco, the two search the estate, inside and out, as rain turns from misty sprinkles to a downpour. Irene is nowhere to be found and Laura’s concern has morphed into fear, verging on panic. She receives a text that states that Irene has been taken and the kidnappers demand $300,000 euros as ransom and warning to not contact the police or Irene will be harmed. At this point the narrative dramatically changes from a light, interesting look at a Spanish family gathering for a wedding to something sinister. It is a mystery that initially focused on where Irene is, and how, absent the police, to possibly get her back. Surprisingly, the crime soon becomes almost secondary to a granular examination of individual family members. What is of apparent interest to writer/director Farhadi is how old grievances, latent animosities and unresolved grudges suddenly emerge as the tensions swirl around the hunt for Irene. The focus turns to the family’s interactions. They don’t coalesce around the need to find Irene (who is asthmatic) but spend time on unresolved familial issues causing Laura, now looking haunted and in full despair, to often remark to family members, “This is not the time.” And yet this is the geography of human behavior that most interests Farhadi, not the whodunit aspects nut drifting toward understanding relationships that, under stress, begin to crumble. The kidnapping becomes a crucible that is decidedly unflattering. To his credit, Farhadi doesn’t allow the years-ago romance between Paco and Laura to rekindle, even when she feels turning to him to help recover Irene is her only option. What makes Everyone Knows exceptional are the fine performances by a very strong ensemble, led by Penelope Cruz’s powerful portrayal of a fragmenting mother. Complementing Cruz is Javier Bardem, who convincingly inhabits the deeply conflicted Paco, suddenly overwhelmed by a secret told to him by Laura that he never saw coming. During the denouement, there are many opportunities for the family to question Irene about her captors, or simply question her for details and clues. For reasons that are consistent with their involvement from the outset, the family asks nothing of Irene, and so Laura, Alejandro and their children leave to return to Argentina. If there was family complicity in the kidnapping, no one is especially interested. Not even Paco, who loses a great deal, asks that essential question: Who? Everybody Knows. articles.text: Review and essay by Anastasia Edel As an ex-Soviet myself, I am baffled by the renewed global fascination with autocracy. According to Freedom House, 8 out of 10 people now live in a partly free or not free country. In the United States, surveys show that a substantial number of people would support authoritarian rule and do not consider the decline of democratic institutions a mortal threat. In China, Russia, and elsewhere, the winds of change seem to be blowing in the wrong direction. Given this shift, HBO’s miniseries The Regime, whose finale aired on April 7, could not have been timelier. With Emmy Award-winning Kate Winslet and Succession’s Will Tracy at the helm, along with all the trappings of prestige television, The Regime was poised to explore some of the 21st century’s heftiest political questions: the allure of demagogues, the slide into unfreedom and tribalism, and the mechanisms a society can employ to reverse this slide. Instead, The Regime provides only vague winks to the tendencies of the world’s strongmen that fail to rise to the level of serious critique or analysis, deployed with a naivete that feels distinctly American. Winslet stars as Elena Vernham, a middle-aged chancellor of an unnamed fictitious country in Central Europe who is obsessed with the black mold she believes is invading her palace. To fight it, she summons Herbert Zubak (Matthias Schoenaerts), a hunky army corporal from a province that grows sugar beets. Prior to his arrival at the palace, Herbert was thrust into the national limelight for his role in gunning down 12 protesters at one of the country’s cobalt mines, earning him a gruesome nickname: “The Butcher.” Elena and Herbert quickly develop a Beauty and the Beast kind of attraction (postmodern, of course, with no clarity about who is the beast—capricious and delusional Elena or self-loathing, bullied-turned-bully Herbert). After a brief falling out, resolved by Herbert saving Elena from an assassin, the two begin to rule the palace through a Rasputin-style combination of hysterics and nativism. For the next five episodes, we follow Herbert’s zigzagging ascent through Elena’s wobbling realm, from a walking humidity monitor to a trusted political advisor and lover. Herbert witnesses, engages in, or directs various antics that, according to the show’s description, depict a “modern authoritarian regime as it unravels.” Scenes include cabinet meetings that Elena conducts from an ice-filled tub and bizarre conversations with her dead father, preserved in a glass coffin in the palace’s basement. Herbert, a man of rural origins, caters to Elena’s paranoia by cleansing the palace’s supposedly poisonous air with the steam from boiled potatoes (a folk remedy popular in my Soviet childhood). Of course, no leader can outrun geopolitics. The country’s rich cobalt reserves attract international interest, and after chasing out a deal that would have given the United States mining rights on the cheap, Elena cozies up to China, promising it a free trade deal and a cut of the minKate Winslet in The Regime ing profits. Together, Elena and Herbert then navigate their way through the illegal annexation of a sovereign neighbor, a halfbaked flirtation with nationalization and land reform, and the sting of Western economic sanctions. All this chaotic politicking unfolds against Elena’s droning on about love, which she constantly either bestows on or demands from her people. articles.text: Charming Montclair Village is the perfect spot to take a break from the bustle of the Bay during the Montclair Village Art Walk. This sidewalk art show celebrates art in the outdoors with more than 40 artists from the Bay Area displaying their handcrafted works. Support the artists the weekend of April 20-21 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. each day. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this free open air art gallery offers a chance to get to know the participating artists and learn the stories behind each piece they make. Among the artisans this year’s event are: Brad Berkheimer Abstract Art Brad Berkheimer has been a full-time professional decorative painter in the Monterey and Pebble Beach areas for over 40 years, specialized in many types of faux finishes, decorative painting of home interior spaces, and custom automotive painting and graphics. He transitioned those skills and experiences to find renewed joy and inspiration in the painting of original abstract artwork on canvas. “My art is guided by the forms, textures, colors and movement I find in Nature,” says Brad. “I look to create unique organic images that attempt to mimic a full spectrum of tones, dynamics and harmonic corrosion found in the natural world.” David Bowman Metal Art Consisting of David Mills Bowman and his son, Reed Christopher Bowman, David M Bowman Studio produces a range of functional and decorative metal artwork. These talented artists collaborate on the design and creation of a wide range of pieces including wall art, vases and candle holders. They construct all of the pieces by hand, with hand tools and simple machines. All the work is produced from brass and copper sheet and rod, formed into shape with shears, hammers, sanders and grinders, and brazed together using an oxyacetylene welding torch. The two do not cast work or use cast parts and they mix patina chemicals from scratch and apply them by hand. Jacque Price Paintings Jacque Price paints in oil using brush and knife, and she often incorporates oil sticks to create meandering lines that silhouette forms or ridge lines. Her process of toning the canvas in a myriad of colors when she first starts a painting sets the groundwork for creating a workable composition that then leads to inspired contextual forms in the final layers. Jacque’s current body of work is curious in nature - amorphous shapes encompass figures in contemplation, ambiguous compositions disperse focus, emotion and stillness meet along lines of vivid color. Her work reveals skill in rendering, an understanding of design, and a proclivity for nature and its influence on the human experience. Doug Rubenstein Ceramics Doug Rubenstein is a potter who uses clay as his primary medium. His work spans a range of creations and sizes. On the small side, he sells dishes, jewelry holders, salt cellars, breakfast bowls, mugs, and tumblers. The medium items include ramen bowls, side plates, dinner plates, jars and pasta bowls. Larger items are vases and serving bowls. “I like to think of my artwork as part of a fifth season - or a season of feeling - honoring, digesting and fathoming that which the world unfolds for us each year,” says Doug. “I design with aesthetics and textures that respect, pay homage and connect to nature while exploring the marriage between natural materials and man-made tools.” Visit these and other talented artists at the Montclair Village Art Walk which takes place on Mountain Boulevard at LaSalle Avenue. For more information, contact the Montclair Village Association at (510) 339-1000 or Pacific Fine Arts Festivals at (209) 267-4394, www. pacificfinearts.com. Presented by

articles.text: It was sunny and warm for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday on April 10, and there was a big turnout of 45 walkers and two K-9 best friends to enjoy it. The group went to the Davie Tennis Stadium last September, but it was “temporarily closed” in February by the City of Oakland after storms knocked down a eucalyptus tree near the courts. After some local news coverage, the stadium was finally reopened. The walkers hadn’t been inside since June 2022, so it was time for a revisit. An eastern dogwood behind the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park was in peak bloom and provided a good start. The group made their way up the hill to Guilford Road and took an almost hidden path to Hazel Lane and then Requa Road with clear views of San Francisco and Wildwood Avenue. At the steps above Witter Field, they saw a Heritage Tree, an eastern redbud, which the group hadn’t seen before. The group continued on to Prospect Road, Oakmont Avenue, and down Oak Road to the entrance of the stadium. The smell of eucalyptus trees that surround the stadium welcomed them. Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research reported that Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area, established a nursery near Mountain View Cemetery in the second half of the 19th Century and sold eucalyptus seedlings. Frank C. Havens also brought eucalyptus to the area from Australia thinking their wood would be a fast-growing building material replacement for the redwoods that were cut down during the late 19th and early 20th-century for home building. Unfortunately, the eucalyptus wood was generally not suitable for lumber as it is heavy and shrinks when dry, which can cause splitting and cracking. Stone quarries were an important part of Oakland’s growth and development. In the city’s earliest days, construction materials like stone blocks and paving stones were imported as sailing-ship ballast around Cape Horn. Oakland’s geologic variability, because it is near the edge of a continental plate, provided a variety of construction materials from surface deposits and outcroppings. Since much of Oakland’s period of most rapid growth occurred prior to the adoption of asphalt in the 1920s, macadam was used extensively in road building. This led to many quarries throughout the area. A quarry at what is now the Davie Stadium was opened in 1878 by the Alameda Macadamizing Company and reopened as the Piedmont Paving Company in about 1892. The land was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by former Oakland mayor John L. Davie. The facility was built in 1936-1937 as a WPA project. The land is primarily in Piedmont, but Davie giving it to Oakland probably explains why the stadium is managed by the City of Oakland. The walkers were impressed by the steep cliffs from the old quarry that surround the courts, but erosion and fallen eucalyptus are evident. Unfortunately, the vintage 1920s clubhouse was locked and the walkers couldn’t go inside to see its pictures and memorabilia. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register with the Recreation Department at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: As the families of elderly parents celebrate Mother’s Day on Sunday, May 12, there are many options for activities and gifts that can bring joy to all involved. As people age, the ultimate expression of love is the way they care for others. This could be an elderly wife caring for her ailing husband, or an adult daughter providing care for her ill mother. This makes celebrating Mother’s Day more difficult than it used to be. One option for a Mother’s Day gift comes in the form of respite care. By finding a temporary stand-in caregiver for a loved one, it gives the adult daughter or older wife a much-needed break. Sometimes a few hours of refreshing separation can be the most help. There are also several other ideas for possible gifts and activities families can try that can make for an enjoyable experience. Activities: • Go for a scenic drive or tour old neighborhoods. These trips to beautiful locations or down memory lane can lead to meaningful discussions and stories. • Create a scrapbook. Going through old photos and recipes and putting them into a book is a fun activity and it creates a treasured item along the way. • Go to church or temple. This may be something that is difficult to do on a regular basis, so going on Mother’s Day is rewarding spiritually and it allows your elderly mother to connect with friends. • Spend a day working on the yard or in the garden. While your mother may not physically be able to do yard work anymore, she will appreciate spending time outside with you as you work to make the view out her window more beautiful. • Play games or put together puzzles. These group activities are full of fun. They keep your mother’s mind active, but do not tax her physically. • Ask for help. By involving your elderly mother in any activity, she feels needed. Depending on her physical abilities, you can cook together or work in the garden. Start by asking what she would like to do. Gifts: • Give your elderly mother the latest large-print book by their favorite author or enroll them in a large-print book club. If that is not an option, a magnifying glass can go a long way. • Buy clothes that are easy to get on and off. Using these items helps your elderly mother retain independence because it is something she can do easily herself. If the mock-buttons or snaps are hidden by panels, these clothes can still look fashionable and don’t let others know about your mother’s struggle with dressing herself. • Get a foot massager or portable foot bath with whirlpool. This can help if your mother complains of tired or aching feet. • Sign up your mother for a Netflix subscription or for another movie service. If your mom loves the Hollywood classics, this can give her the opportunity to once again enjoy the films she loved during her youth. The whole family can watch the films together and it becomes a gift that keeps on giving. • Get your mother a subscription to a magazine. There are many magazines devoted to senior health and travel. These can provide a sense of empathy and valuable information. Ask your mother what sort of magazines she would enjoy reading regularly. • Get your mom a spa package that can include a massage, a facial, a manicure and/or a pedicure. Check to see if the spa caters to elderly clients. This sort of rejuvenation could be just what your mother needs. Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I will be traveling a lot this summer, and I want to make sure I have the right settings to make my iPhone safer. I will be in several countries and don’t plan to take my computer. Also, is there a way to have access to files on my computer? Gerry, Piedmont Dear Gerry: More and more people are leaving their larger laptops and even iPads at home when they travel and just using their phones. Luckily you can do most everything you need on your phone these days. Let’s take your last question first. If you have iCloud Desktop and Documents enabled, which means that your data that is stored on your desktop and in your documents folder is also backed up onto iCloud, you can access these files through your phone app called, “Files.” It looks like a little blue folder and if you open that app, you can browse through items in your document folder as well as in your desktop. This is handy in case you are away from home and unexpectedly need a file that is stored on your computer. Once you find that file, you can email it, send it via a message and even edited it. If you use Microsoft Office, you can install the iPhone version and that would allow you to edit a Microsoft Word or Excel file. There are also other apps that more and more can make your iPhone like a mini computer. One of them is called Genius Scan. This allows you to scan documents with your phone, and then share them via email or text message. I have this app and find myself using this much more than my fancy document scanner. One of the features that I like is this. If you need to scan a document that has been folded, so it doesn’t like quite flat, this application actually flattens it out in the scan. If you must sign a document that you have scanned with your phone, you can use an app like Signeasy or Acrobat mobile. Now for your first question about making sure your iPhone is secure when you travel. There are a few settings that can help your phone be secure. Of course you must be vigilant, don’t do banking on local Wi-Fi if possible, and if you’re in a country that has a lot of theft, keep your phone out of view. If you are riding in a cab, don’t keep your phone next to you on the seat with the window open. Now for some good security settings. 1 If you haven’t already set a passcode, do so. And if you have a four digit passcode, set a six digit one. And make sure it is a secure one, not something like 000000, or 123456. 2. Use Face ID or Touch ID if you have an older phone. 3. Make sure that you have Find My iPhone enabled. This helps to prevent anyone else from activating your phone or using it. You can sign into your iCloud account from another device, even another phone that has “find my iPhone,” with your Apple ID, and disable, your missing iPhone. You can even create a message that will display on the screen with a phone number to reach you. 4. Turn on Stolen Device Protection. This is a security feature that has been added and is a no-brainer when you’re traveling and even when you’re not. This protects your phone in case someone who has stolen it can figure out or knows your passcode. With this feature activated many actions require you to use Face ID or Touch ID. And even more sensitive operations require a security delay. For iPhones with Face ID, go to Settings/ Face ID & Passcode and enter your passcode/ scroll down to Stolen Device Protection. Tap to turn it on. There are a couple of options with this. If you only want it activated when you are away, tap “Away from Familiar Locations.” And if you want to just have this on all the time, tap “Always.” 5. Use “Safety Check.” This allows you to review the information that you share with people and apps. You can go here to immediately stop sharing information. 6. Control app tracking. However, his achievements were monumental, including expansive upgrades to Versailles and Louvre palaces – contributions of permanence and extraordinary beauty, and singularly French. Toward the end of his reign, the Sun King’s shine lost some of its glow: critics gained traction about cost overages and extravagant expenditures; depleted royal coffers; and taxes that fell too heavily on an exhausted populace. Sometime in the 1690s the war gods abandoned Louis, and he ultimately suffered a series of defeats at the hands of England’s greatest general, John Churchill, who Queen Anne rewarded by naming him the First Duke of Marlborough. His greatest victory over the French was the Battle of Blenheim. As the end of Louis’s life, three of his heir-apparent successors – his son, grandson, and elder great-grandson – were all struck down with fatal illnesses within one year. Louis XV reigned for the next 59 years, a span second only to that of Louis XIV, but he did not take his great-grandfather’s advice on war. He began waging war in 1756 on two continents: The Seven Years’ War in Europe where France fought Great Britain and Prussia; and in North America, where France was engaged in the French and Indian War and allied with American natives against the British. They are experts at finding sweet-smelling flowers after dark. As such, they contribute to the health of green pastures. The New York Times reports that air pollution might be making flowers less attractive to pollinators like hawk moths. Compounds called nitrate radicals can severely degrade the scent emitted by the pale evening primrose, one of the favorite flowers of hawk mothers. The less fragrant flowers may ultimately mean less hawk moths, which in turn will mean fewer green pastures which in turn undermines our personal well-being. And so, this once fearful, contrary girl must face the museum-like, harrowing, spirit-filled place and learn to be brave for the sake of herself and her parents. Ultimately, it is her transformation that is at the center of the story. The animation is rich, lush and soft, each frame a hand drawn work of art. The story is unusual, But there is no fear in Elena’s kingdom. Her out-of-grace oligarch is not dispossessed and jailed but simply ordered to clean up chairs at a press conference. Her ministers plot for her downfall in a downstairs bar before mockingly denying her a seat on the rescue helicopter. The rebels take the palace in a span of an episode. (If only real dictators were toppled that easily!) The Regime makes Elena look stupid and pathetic. We do not flee from her in terror; we shrug her off. Despite her European aesthetics, the portrayal of Elena as a ruler reflects an undeniably American attitude toward autocracy.
